Towards a Classification of Holographic Multi-partite Entanglement Measures

From permutation invariants to weighted cosmic-brane webs that probe holographic geometry.

arXiv:2304.06082 · Published: JHEP 08 (2023) 202 · INSPIRE · All publications

Looking beyond one entanglement surface

In holography, ordinary entanglement entropy connects a boundary quantum state to the area of a minimal surface in a gravitational spacetime. That connection is powerful, but it begins with a division into only two parties. A state split among several regions has many additional patterns of correlation. This paper develops a framework for asking which multipartite quantities admit similarly useful geometric descriptions and which can probe the original bulk geometry, rather than requiring a completely new gravitational solution.

The difference between probing and backreacting is already present for two parties. A Rényi entropy at a general replica index requires a geometry with a finite conical defect. Taking the appropriate limit removes that defect and gives a minimal-area quantity in the original spacetime. The paper seeks multipartite analogues of this mechanism, starting from local-unitary invariants of a pure state and organizing them into families that admit a suitable continuation.

A general invariant is built by contracting copies of the wavefunction with conjugate copies. Each party contributes a permutation specifying how its indices are paired. This description supports both classification and counting: disconnected contraction diagrams factorize, while connected diagrams supply the basic building blocks. There are rapidly growing numbers of possibilities, so geometric usefulness provides an extra selection principle. The classification uses local-unitary invariance to organize the boundary observables, while the probe condition selects those with a particularly direct geometric interpretation.

A particularly tractable family comes from independent cyclic permutations assigned to the parties. The replica data are expressed using integer labels, and special families interpolate toward a probe limit. This construction extends the earlier multi-entropy and allows different pieces of the eventual bulk network to carry different weights. It turns the search for one privileged multipartite number into a structured collection of boundary observables.

The replica construction and its weighted geometric answer

To compute these quantities in a field theory, copies of a Euclidean path integral are glued according to their permutations. The resulting replicated boundary is filled by a gravitational saddle. The decisive assumption is that its dominant filling preserves the boundary replica symmetry. When it does, the bulk can be quotiented to a simpler geometry containing conical singularities, with each singular segment associated with a boundary-region interface.

The corresponding cosmic-brane contribution is:

\[ \displaystyle{\mathcal{S}}_{\rm br}^{(k)}=\frac{k-1}{4kG_{N}}\int dy^{D-1}\sqrt{h}=\frac{k-1}{4kG_{N}}A \]

The cone order sets the brane tension, the induced metric measures its worldvolume, and the area factor makes the geometric content explicit. Continuing toward the probe limit sends the backreaction away. A network of weighted minimal surfaces then remains in the unreplicated geometry. Figure 1 shows the boundary regions and the corresponding bulk chambers, whose separating walls form the web.

The area functional is determined by a weighted minimization:

\[ \displaystyle\partial_{n}{\mathcal{S}}_{\rm grav}|_{n=1}=\frac{1}{4G_{N}}{\rm min}_{\cal W}\left\{\sum_{\widetilde{L}_{\sigma_{\mathtt{a}}^{-1}\sigma_{\mathtt{b}}}\in{\mathcal{W}}}\log({\rm lcm}(m_{\mathtt{a}},m_{\mathtt{b}}))A_{{\mathtt{a}},{\mathtt{b}}}\right\}\equiv\frac{1}{4G_{N}}A_{\rm min}^{\cal W}. \]

Here the weights are logarithms of least common multiples of the integer party labels. They are fixed by the replica construction rather than chosen by hand. Minimization includes the allowed arrangement of the web, not merely the position of one preselected junction. The resulting probe measure has the compact form:

\[ \displaystyle S^{\{m_{\mathtt{a}}\}}=\frac{1}{4G_{N}}A_{\rm min}^{\cal W}. \]

This is the multipartite geometric prescription: a weighted area divided by the gravitational coupling. In three bulk dimensions, the areas reduce to lengths of geodesic segments. As an explicit example, the equal-label three-party case reduces to a junction problem. For equal labels, the measure becomes:

\[ \displaystyle S^{\{m,m,m\}}=\frac{\log m}{4G_{N}}{\rm min}_{X}\Big(\sum_{i}\ell(P_{i},X))\Big). \]

The boundary endpoints are fixed while the interior junction is optimized. Unequal labels generalize the competition among the segments. This makes the geometric meaning of the boundary family concrete: changing the observable changes the web’s tensions and therefore which portions of spacetime it probes.

The paper tests the prescription against two-dimensional CFT calculations involving twist-operator correlation functions and semiclassical conformal blocks. The dependence on boundary positions, including the nontrivial cross-ratio dependence, agrees in the cases analyzed. Three-point coefficients of twist operators supply the remaining normalization data, while the bulk junction calculation predicts their contribution to the probe measure. For four and five connected regions, the calculations also test how this constant contribution scales with the number of trivalent vertices.

Replica geometries and finer bulk partitions

Different choices of multipartite measure can draw different webs across the same spacetime. Overlaying them partitions a bulk slice more finely than a single bipartite entanglement wedge does. Figure 2 displays this refinement for several probe webs. Regions inaccessible to one boundary party can be subdivided by observables sensitive to several parties together, motivating questions about a more detailed account of bulk locality.

This geometric refinement suggests a connection to quantum error correction. A bulk region in the entanglement shadow can be reconstructed jointly from certain pairs of boundary parties, even when it lies outside the entanglement wedge of each party separately. Multipartite webs subdivide that shadow, distinguishing regions that share the same bipartite reconstruction description. The paper proposes that multipartite analogues of mutual information could help express the corresponding finer reconstruction properties.

The replica geometry can be studied explicitly in low-genus cases. For three parties at replica index three, the replicated boundary is a torus at a symmetric point in moduli space. Several equally short cycles are exchanged by the replica group, and choosing one to contract in the bulk breaks part of the symmetry. For four parties at index two, the replicated boundary is a rectangular torus. Its independent cycles are preserved by the replica action, allowing an explicit replica-symmetric dominant filling. These examples reveal how cycle structure controls the symmetry of the saddle.

The continuation toward the probe limit connects this discrete replica data to continuous geometric tensions. The paper examines the growth conditions associated with uniqueness of analytic continuation and uses generalized GHZ states to illustrate the structure of the boundary problem. In the semiclassical bulk, the continued conical defects become weighted probe surfaces. Together, the permutation classification, replica-symmetric derivation, and CFT checks establish a systematic framework for relating families of multipartite observables to networks within a single gravitational spacetime.
